notes.meaning: David resolved to guard his actions and keep a tight muzzle on his mouth. He knew ungodly people were watching him closely, ready to twist his words. Rather than risk sinning by complaining about God's ways in front of them, he decided to stay completely silent.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine took the name Jeduthun to mean "leaping over them." To him it pictures any believer who rises above people whose hearts are set on passing earthly things.

notes.meaning: David kept absolute silence, holding back even good and fitting words. Instead of easing his pain, keeping his grief locked up inside only stirred up his sorrow and made it worse. Total silence proved too heavy a burden for him to bear.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early church teacher Augustine wrote that David made a mistake by withholding good speech out of fear of evil, and later came to regret his total silence.

notes.meaning: Holding back his feelings caused an inner fire to build up inside David's heart. The more he quietly brooded over his hardships, the hotter his distress burned. At last, he could no longer hold his peace, and the smothered flame broke out into speech.

differ.view: Some evangelicals believe David did not break his good promise here. He only stopped holding back good words, and the first thing he said was a prayer.

notes.meaning: Instead of venting his frustration to people, David turned his speech upward in prayer to God. He asked the Lord to help him realize how short his earthly life is and how soon it will end. Knowing his own human weakness would help him keep his troubles in proper perspective.

differ.view: Some evangelicals read this as a tired, impatient wish. David was weary of suffering and wanted to know how long he had left to bear it.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine took "my end" to mean the goal not yet reached. It is the prize Paul pressed toward, beyond this life of trials.

notes.meaning: David observes that God has measured out human life to just a handbreadth, a short span of a few inches. Compared to God's endless eternity, a person's entire lifetime seems like nothing at all. Even people in their best and strongest state are as fleeting as a single breath.

Human beings rush around chasing earthly goals, but they are like shadows living in an imaginary world. They exhaust themselves with endless activity and pile up wealth, yet life is so uncertain that they cannot know who will take their riches when they are gone.

Seeing the emptiness and shortness of worldly life helps David reorient his thoughts. He asks what he is truly waiting for, knowing that earthly things cannot satisfy. He places his full hope and expectation in God alone.

differ.view: Some evangelicals believe David did not yet have a clear hope of life after death. Even facing death, he simply threw himself on the living God.

notes.meaning: David turns to God for rescue from all his sins, recognizing that his distress came from his own wrongdoing. He also begs the Lord to spare him from being mocked and disgraced by foolish, ungodly people.

David falls silent again, but this time it is a quiet submission rather than bitter frustration. He refuses to complain, because he knows that his suffering has come from God's own sovereign hand. Recognizing God's purpose in his trials brings him peace.

David asks the Lord to take away the painful blow of His discipline. He feels like a wounded fighter who cannot keep going against such overwhelming strength. He knows he will quickly perish if God does not show mercy and lift His hand.

When God corrects a person for sin, His discipline consumes everything that person prizes, just as a hidden moth quietly ruins fine clothes. Human beauty, strength, and pride melt away before God's judgment. This shows once more that every person is nothing more than a passing vapor.

David pleads with God to hear his prayer, listen to his desperate cry, and notice his tears. He reminds the Lord that he is only a foreigner and a temporary guest on the earth, walking in need of God's care just like his ancestors did.

David asks God to turn His stern, frowning gaze away so he can catch his breath and find joy again. He desires a brief season of restored strength before his life here ends and he passes away from this world.

differ.view: Some evangelicals see these words as partly coming from deep sorrow that went too far. It shows how hard it is for believers to keep their words measured when death seems close.
